title: Fast capacity bridge and graceful failover - runbook draft
content:
Purpose:
This is a working draft for rapid capacity bridging and graceful failover when GPU nodes fail, manifesting as CUDA device errors, NVLink flaps, or complete node eviction. The goal: keep model-serving availability within SLO while minimizing wasted cost and avoiding noisy rollbacks.

Audience:
Primary: on-call SREs and infra engineers performing emergency GPU replacements, node cordon/drain, quick capacity add, and cluster recovery. Secondary: release engineers and solutions eng who need to understand temporary capacity modes.

High-level strategy (short):
- Detect -> isolate -> redirect traffic to healthy pools -> add temporary capacity (ephemeral or warm nodes) -> perform safe GPU cartridge swap and node remediation -> reintroduce node after sanity checks -> decommission temporary capacity.
- Prefer capacity-bridging (bring up warm ephemeral nodes in same AZ/zone) to avoid cross-zone KV/cache churn.

Signal definitions / run triggers:
- P1: >=5% error rate increase on generation endpoints for >2m AND median latency > 2x baseline on /v1/generate endpoints.
- P1 alt: Pod eviction with CrashLoopBackOff for model-serving pods and node marked NotReady for >3m.
- Slack alert channel: #sre-oncall -> escalate to #platform-incident if customer-facing impact.

Initial triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
1) Identify scope
   - Which nodes show GPU errors? kubectl get nodes -o wide | grep -E "gpu|g4|a100"
   - Check node conditions: kubectl describe node <node> (Look for MemoryPressure, DiskPressure, NetworkUnavailable)
   - Confirm which daemonsets/pods are affected: kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep <node>
2) Validate alerts and traces
   - Look at console metrics: generation error rate, queue depth, per-node GPU utilization in Lumberjack dashboard.
   - Check tracing traces for timeouts/slowdowns in frontends -> inference proxies -> sharders.
3) Communicate
   - Post short summary in #sre-oncall: what, where, immediate impact, who is on it. Tag @oncall.
   - Open an incident ticket (prefilled template): JIRA-INC-<timestamp> and link to runbook.

Safe isolation (cordon + controlled drain)
- Goal: Remove node from scheduler quickly while minimizing in-flight request loss and KV cache thrash.
- Commands: (feel free to paste in Terminal)
   kubectl cordon <node>  # marks unschedulable
   kubectl drain <node> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --grace-period=120 --timeout=10m --pod-selector='app!=infra-proxy'
- Notes: Use --pod-selector to preserve infra-proxy/sidecar pods that must remain for network path. If drain hangs because of long-running model jobs, use kubectl delete pod --force --grace-period=0 as last resort after notifying product-owner and documenting lost requests.
- For high-priority serving classes, prefer to route traffic first (see Traffic redirection) and then drain.

Traffic redirection (quick paths):
- If routing layer supports tag-based fallback: add rule to route model=redwood-latest -> fallback-model=redwood-small for best-effort continuity.
- If service mesh: apply desired DestinationRule to reduce maxRetries to 3 and send new sessions to healthy subset.
- If immediate capacity shortfall: raise ephemeral capacity pool: opsctl scale pool ephemeral-gpu --zone <zone> --count <n> --instance-type p3dn or a100s-rt. Default start: +2 nodes per 100 QPS deficit (heuristic).

Ephemeral capacity bring-up (fast path):
- Use the hot-warm images from infra-bastion: ami-inference-warm:2024-09.
- opsctl preview-template ephemeral-node --zone <zone> --image ami-inference-warm:2024-09 --gpu-type a100 --init-script scripts/warm-init.sh
- opsctl create fleet --template ephemeral-node --count 2 --labels temporary=bridge,managed-by=opsctl
- Wait for bootstrap: kubectl get nodes --selector temporary=bridge -w
- Verify: GPU visible (nvidia-smi), kubelet ready, node GPU plugin logs OK.

GPU cartridge swap (hardware replacement) - field tech steps (summary for oncall to coordinate with data-center tech):
- Safety: power down node properly, log serial console. Ensure ESD precautions and proper mounting torque when replacing card.
- Swap order: power off node -> unlock blade -> remove failed GPU -> insert replacement -> reseat power connectors -> power on -> watch boot and bios for GPU enumeration.
- BIOS tips: If GPU not enumerating, check PCIe bifurcation settings and reset to defaults, reflash if previous firmware mismatch suspected.
- Post-swap checks (oncall): ssh to node, run nvidia-smi; run small workload in staging namespace to confirm CUDA kernels load and remote KV warmups proceed.

Cluster recovery and cache warming strategy:
- Avoid full-slab cache flush. Instead: as nodes rejoin, rehydrate model KV caches gradually by scheduling warmup jobs: 
   - kubectl apply -f warmup-job.yaml --env MODEL=redwood-llm-1 --replicas=2
- Monitor p99 latencies to ensure no spike. Use slowdown windows to stagger warmups across AZs.

Rollback and fall-forward decision matrix:
- If error rate remains >3% after 15m of fixes and warmups: consider rolling traffic to alternative model family (smaller quantized) with explicit customer SLO notice.
- If hardware swap fails or more nodes fail in same rack: escalate to infra team, consider evacuating rack and routing traffic to other racks.

Post-incident tasks (within 48h):
- Capture timeline and key decisions in incident ticket.
- Export logs and attach kernel messages (dmesg), nvidia bugreport logs, and kube events.
- Follow-up action items: firmware roll, replace all cards from same lot, update node-boot image to include NVLink timeout patches.

Quick checks and useful commands (clipboard-friendly):
- kubectl get nodes --selector=gpu=true -o wide
- kubectl describe node <node> | egrep -i "Condition:|Taint|PodCIDR"
- kubectl get pods -o wide --all-namespaces | grep <node>
- ssh core@<node> 'sudo journalctl -u kubelet -n 200'
- ssh core@<node> 'sudo /usr/local/bin/nvidia-bug-report.sh --output /tmp/bugreport.tar.gz'

Communication templates (short):
- Slack initial: "P1: Node <node> experiencing GPU errors -> cordoned. Impact: ~X% of generation capacity in zone <z>. Oncall: @maya. Triage started. Inc ticket: JIRA-INC-2045"
- Customer note (if public incident): "We are aware of increased latency/errors for model generation in region X; engineers are performing controlled failover and capacity injection. We will share updates every 15 minutes until resolved."

Open questions / TODOs (document owner action items):
- Define exact autoscale policy for ephemeral pool (current heuristic is guesswork).
- Add a safe drain mode that increments graceful-period across pods to reduce forced deletions.
- Validate warm-init image across all GPU types (a100/p4/p3).
- Add automated warmup job sizing by model token/sec.

Appendix: Known gotchas and mitigations
- NVSwitch flapping can present as partial GPU visibility; rebooting the node often masks the underlying fabric degradation. If repeat, escalate for hardware replacement and avoid repeated reboots (burns PMs).
- Draining large-stateful model loaders will cause long-term cache misses; always prefer ephemeral capacity first when QPS impact is high.
- Cross-zone warmups cause cache thrash; favor same-AZ ephemeral nodes.

Notes to self (rough):
- Keep this doc short and link to longer deep-dive for hardware techs.
- Convert to checklist format for pager rotation later.

History/log:
- 2024-10-03: initial draft (Maya)
- 2024-11-10: added ephemeral capacity commands and hotfix guidance (Diego)
- 2024-11-15: added final communication templates and TODOs (Priya)
